Chapter 8: The Legacy of Fear—How the System Endures
Even after people leave the world of intelligence behind, the system they once served keeps its grip on the country. The legacy of fear? It doesn’t just vanish. It lingers in everyday life—in the words people choose, in the way they glance over their shoulders, and even in how parents teach their kids to watch what they say.
Across Syrian neighborhoods, you can feel the agency’s presence, even when its officers are nowhere to be seen. Folks learn early on to censor themselves, steer clear of certain topics, and only trust those who’ve truly earned it over years. The memories of betrayals—neighbors who disappeared overnight, friends who turned out to be informants—those memories cast a shadow that just won’t go away.
Picture this: There’s a family, once close-knit and open, but everything changes after a relative is arrested. Suddenly, conversations get quiet and careful. Laughter fades. The kids pick up on it, learning not to ask questions or do anything that might attract attention. Nobody talks about the fear out loud, but it shapes every single interaction.
The agency’s methods—surveillance, intimidation, turning people into informants—these things got woven into daily life. Even if you’d never worked for the agency, you couldn’t escape its game. People weighed every word, every gesture, every relationship. In the end, the system’s real achievement wasn’t just the information it gathered, but the habits of fear and caution it trained into everyone.
So, what about reform? When it happened, it was usually half-hearted or didn’t last. The agency’s leaders knew their real power came from keeping fear alive. There were always a few brave souls who tried to push back—organizing protests, speaking out. But the risks were huge, and the rewards? Who could say if they’d ever come.
At its core, the legacy of these intelligence services wasn’t just about politics or who held power. It was about trust. Trust that had been shattered—sometimes beyond repair. And rebuilding it? That takes more than new laws or fresh faces in charge. It needs a real change in how people relate to each other. A willingness to let their guard down, even after years of being told not to.
Looking back, it’s clear—the agency’s real legacy wasn’t just in the files it kept or the people it locked away. It was in the culture of fear it left behind. Undoing that legacy... well, that’s the work of generations.
